title: Trail Distance Estimator: Path Length on the Map
description: Estimate a trail's length from its path on the map with the Trail Distance Estimator — waypoint segments summed honestly, switchbacks included. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, four waypoints on a short ridge walk sum to 1.62 km of path while the endpoints sit only 1.34 km apart — the trail is 21% longer than the map's straight line, as trails always are.
quick_answer: The Trail Distance Estimator measures the length of a path drawn or entered as waypoints on the map, summing the great-circle distance of every segment. Trace the route and read its true length in kilometres or miles — the number hikers and trail crews actually walk.

body.t: Trace the route before you walk it and the day gains an honest length — then pair it with elevation context, since a flat 10 miles and a mountainous 10 miles are different days wearing the same number.
Trail races measured by waypoint sums explain why your watch disagrees: GPS sampling cuts corners the estimator keeps, if the waypoints hug the path.

Guidebooks disagree with each other constantly. An independent waypoint sum is the audit that ends the argument at the trailhead.

Four example waypoints (a ridge path sampled from a GPS log) sum to 1.62 km, segment by segment: 0.25 + 0.68 + 0.68 km. Endpoint-to-endpoint is 1.34 km. The 21% difference is why straight-line tools understate every real trail.

The same path traced with two points instead of four collapses to its chord and loses a fifth of its length. On curves, add waypoints until adding more stops changing the total — that convergence is the measurement.

popular_table.note: On the ground, GPS tracks sample every few seconds and still cut sharp corners slightly. Denser waypoints approach the true path; the estimator is exact for the path you give it.

faq: How many waypoints do I need?
Enough that the polyline hugs the path: every switchback turn and curve deserves one. When doubling the points changes the total by under a percent, you have converged.
Why does my GPS watch show a different distance?

Sampling rate, signal noise in trees and gorges, and corner-cutting algorithms all move the total. A careful map trace and a watch recording measure the same trail with different instruments — small disagreements are normal, large ones mean a sparse trace.

The length is horizontal map distance; steep ground adds a little true distance (a 20% grade adds about 2%). Your legs experience the climb as effort, not mileage — plan time with elevation tools alongside.
Trace the outward path and double it — or trace the return too if the route differs. The estimator sums what you give it, symmetrically honest.
Can I estimate a road route this way?

You can trace roads with waypoints, but the dedicated routing tools follow the road network automatically and add travel time. Waypoint tracing shines where no network exists: trails, fields, water, ice.
Both, with feet for short paths — trail culture in the US speaks miles, most of the world kilometres, and the estimator translates without opinion.
